extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literary criticism, rhetoric, and communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for performing and evaluating close-reading style literary criticism (New Criticism) and related rhetorical/semantic methods. Covers methods (Practical Criticism), theoretical tools (semantic triangle, ambiguity, metaphor, tone), pedagogical experiments, and communication advice (feedforward, Basic English).

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading / New Criticism (text-as-autonomous-object)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the close reading of a literary text, especially poetry, to discover how a work of literature functions as a self-contained and self-referential æsthetic object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the formal elements of the text (form, rhythm, ambiguity, allusiveness, tone, etc.) and analyze the text itself rather than authorial intent or external context. Richards' work contributed to the foundations of New Criticism and its methodology of close reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Criticism (anonymized-text pedagogical test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct critical reading without contextual or authorial information to assess likely impediments to an adequate response to a literary text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards removed authorial and contextual information from thirteen poems and asked undergraduates to write interpretations; the experiment revealed the variety and depth of possible textual misreadings. Use anonymized texts to surface stock responses, misreadings, and the limits of interpretive procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision via denotation and connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for precision in communicating meanings by way of denotation and connotation rather than relying on impressionistic or overly abstract critical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish critical precision, examine how words carry both literal (denotation) and associated (connotation) meanings and articulate those distinctions clearly in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/empirical approach to criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ psychological theory and empirical methods to analyze the processes of writing and reading poetry and to ground critical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards drew on psychology (e.g., Sherrington) and empirical study (Practical Criticism) to explain inferior responses and to make criticism more testable; critics may interrogate readers' responses and cognitive processes to support readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory and detection of ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and theorize ambiguity in texts as a central feature affecting multiple readings and interpretive possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards provided theories of ambiguity (a topic also developed by Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity). Criticism should analyze how ambiguity operates and how it generates divergent readings rather than merely treating ambiguity as error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of metaphor, value, and tone (and impediments to adequate response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conceptual tools—metaphor, value, tone, stock response, incipient action, pseudo-statement—to substantiate interpretive criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards offered these categories to explain how texts produce effects and how readers may misread; evaluate presence, interaction, and effects of these features in a poem or prose piece, and watch for 'stock responses' that shortcut interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic reception / harmony (balance of psychological impulses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess aesthetic understanding as deriving from the balance of competing psychological impulses; consider form, value, rhythm, coenesthesia, allusiveness, divergent readings, and belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards' Foundations of Aesthetics frames aesthetic reception as a balance—criticism should attend to those competing elements and how they produce a sense of harmony or dissonance in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic triangle (symbol–thought–referent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze meaning using the semantic triangle: symbol (word), referent (thing in reality), and thought/reference (the intangible idea converging literal word and object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the triangle to show how words come to mean for an individual reader—meaning is mediated by experience and usage, so critical analysis should track how symbol, thought, and referent relate in a text.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Rhetoric: study of misunderstanding and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach rhetoric as 'a study of misunderstanding and its remedies'—study the meaning of parts of discourse and how usage creates meaning, accepting that ambiguity is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than focusing solely on argument mechanics, analyze how words are used in sentences, how meanings are constructed by readers/listeners, and propose remedies to reduce misunderstanding where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedforward (anticipatory revision method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate the effect of one's words by acting as one's own critic—use feedforward as a pretest to predict audience response and revise accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards coined 'feedforward' as a cybernetic concept: writers should pretest and revise to create clearer effects; those who do not use feedforward may seem dogmatic. Apply feedforward iteratively to clarify concepts and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic English (simplified vocabulary for international communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt simplified English (a controlled vocabulary of roughly 850 words) when aiming for international auxiliary-language clarity or broad pedagogical communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards' Basic English proposes limiting vocabulary to increase intelligibility across language backgrounds; use this as a stylistic guideline when accessibility and international comprehension are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat criticism as accountable and testable (avoid purely impressionistic claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make critical claims that can be substantiated rather than relying on impressionistic assertions; analyze observable textual features and readers' responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards argued criticism could be precise and communicable; ground interpretations in textual evidence, psychological insight, and, where possible, empirical observation of reader responses.
